selected.hypothesis: Electrides are distinguished by (1) a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth cations, (2) overall low elemental electronegativity, (3) the absence of a neutral oxidation‑state assignment (excess electrons), and (4) the presence of large interstitial voids that can host anionic electrons.

final_fit.note: Model fitted on all labeled structures; probability >= 0.5 means electride. Missing feature values are imputed with the median of these structures.

leaderboard.hypothesis: Electrides are distinguished by (1) a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth cations, (2) overall low elemental electronegativity, (3) the absence of a neutral oxidation‑state assignment (excess electrons), and (4) the presence of large interstitial voids that can host anionic electrons.

Electrides are favoured by (i) very low minimum electronegativity, (ii) a high fraction of alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, (iii) a low transition‑metal site fraction that discourages covalent electron binding, (iv) at least one large interstitial cavity, and (v) a high number of geometrically accessible void candidates that provide a rich interstitial network.

Electrides are favoured by (i) very low minimum elemental electronegativity (strongly electropositive cations), (ii) a high fraction of alkali/alkaline‑earth sites (abundant electron donors), (iii) at least one large interstitial cavity, (iv) a generally open void network reflected in a high mean sampled clearance, and (v) a rich set of geometrically viable interstitial sites.

Electrides are identified by (i) low minimum electronegativity indicating electropositive cations, (ii) a high fraction of alkali/alkaline‑earth sites providing excess electrons, (iii) a large maximum interstitial clearance ensuring at least one suitable cavity, (iv) a high mean sampled clearance reflecting overall void openness, and (v) a high standard deviation of sampled clearances indicating heterogeneous cavity sizes that can trap localized electrons.

Electrides are favored by (1) very low minimum electronegativity (strongly electropositive cations), (2) a high fraction of alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, (3) a limited proportion of transition‑metal sites (excess d‑block content suppresses interstitial electrons), (4) the presence of at least one large interstitial cavity, and (5) overall low packing density (large volume per atom).

Electrides are distinguished by a high fraction of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth cations, low minimum elemental electronegativity, a low packing density (high volume per atom), and an open interstitial network evidenced by large maximum clearance and high mean sampled clearance.

Electrides are favoured by (1) very low minimum electronegativity (strong electropositive cations), (2) a high fraction of alkali/alkaline‑earth sites (electron donors), (3) a loosely packed lattice (large volume per atom), (4) at least one large interstitial cavity, and (5) a rich network of accessible void sites (high candidate count), all of which together promote stabilization of interstitial anionic electrons.

Electrides are favoured by very low minimum electronegativity, a high fraction of alkali/alkaline‑earth sites, overall lattice openness, a rich network of accessible interstitial sites, and a heterogeneous void‑size distribution that provides sufficiently large cavities while maintaining overall openness.
